The Days It Takes To Leave

9 août 20266.5/10

Everyone owns the same names. You have seen the ownership tables where the same handful of megacaps show up in fund after fund, and you have probably felt the quiet worry that comes with it. If they all wanted out at once, could they get out? The question usually gets filed under macro anxiety and forgotten, because it sounds unanswerable. It is answerable. It has a number, the number takes about a minute to compute, and almost nobody bothers to compute it.

The measure is days to exit. Take the dollar value of a fund's position in a stock. Divide it by the average daily dollar volume of that stock. What comes back is the number of sessions it would take to sell the whole line if that fund were the entire tape. The figure is crude by construction, and crude is what makes it useful. It converts a vague sense that a position is big into a length of time, and duration is something you can actually reason about, because duration is exactly what a seller stops controlling once the exit gets crowded.

Then make it realistic. Nobody is the entire tape. Push even a fifth of a stock's daily volume through your own selling and you become the loudest participant in the name, visible to every execution algorithm watching for exactly that, and the price starts moving against you long before you are done. So the honest version of the calculation caps you at a fraction of daily volume, which stretches the exit by a multiple. A line that looks like a week at full volume becomes most of a month at a share you could actually get filled on. That is the figure I care about, and it is the one you should be able to pull for any name you hold.

Most people reach for percent of float instead, or for position weight. Both are weaker. Percent of float tells you what a fund owns of the company and says nothing about whether anyone is trading it this week, since a small float can turn over furiously while a large one sits still. Position weight tells you what the manager has at stake and says nothing about the width of the door. Days to exit is the only one of the three that puts the size of the position and the width of the door into the same fraction. It has one more rare property: you can falsify it tomorrow with a volume feed and a filing, which is more than most positioning analysis can claim.

Run it across the funds worth tracking and the reassuring half of the answer arrives first. The megacaps everyone frets about are the easiest positions on the board to leave. The aggregate holdings in the biggest names clear in days or in a couple of weeks even under a realistic volume cap, because the same crowding that makes them frightening is what makes them liquid. Thousands of participants trade those names all day long. Crowding cuts both ways, and on the way out it is the thing working for you.

The uncomfortable half sits where nobody is looking. The extreme cases are nowhere near the megacaps. They live in the concentrated books, the ones run by managers whose reputations were built on conviction. Carl Icahn's largest line needs the better part of a trading year to unwind at a realistic share of volume, and it accounts for something close to half of everything the fund holds. Fairholme's stake in St. Joe is heavier still: most of the book in a single name, and something on the order of half a year of sessions to get out of it. Those are not positions any more. They are marriages. The manager cannot sell without becoming the price, and becoming the price destroys the value they are trying to harvest.

That is what the metric changes about the way you read a filing. Past a certain exit length, a holding stops behaving like a position and starts behaving like a commitment. My own line sits around forty sessions; put yours wherever you like, the threshold matters less than having one. Above it, the time it takes to leave runs longer than the time most theses stay valid, so the manager is locked into being right. They will defend the name in public because there is no other option available to them. They will add on weakness because adding is cheaper than exiting. And when they finally do leave, you will not read it as a decision, you will read it as months of unexplained heaviness in the tape with no news attached to it. That is the part you can use. Persistent pressure in a thinly traded name with one large concentrated holder is rarely a mystery. It is arithmetic.

The same arithmetic runs through the disclosure delay, and there it cuts deeper. Congressional trades surface on a lag that runs closer to two months than to two weeks once you measure the gap between the transaction date and the day the filing appears. Fund holdings arrive on a quarterly cycle with a reporting window stacked on top. In both cases, by the time you can see the move it has aged past the point where copying it does anything for you. Plenty of strategies get built on this data as though it were a signal. It is a census. A census tells you who was standing where when the count was taken, and the count was taken a long time ago.

So here is what I would watch into the autumn filings. Take any consolidated book you follow, find its largest line, and check the exit length on it. If that line crosses forty sessions at a realistic share of volume, read the manager's public conviction as constrained rather than freely expressed. Then watch two things. Whether the weight of a single name climbs past a quarter of the book, and whether daily volume in that name is drying up while the position stays the same size. The second one is the quiet killer, because exit length is a fraction and the denominator moves on its own. A position that took a month to leave in June can take a season to leave by October without the fund buying a single additional share.

The dashboard does this arithmetic for you. It shows the consolidated book on one line, and behind every ticker the exit length computed against that session's real volume rather than a stale average. Run it on the names you actually hold. The figure that comes back is the one that never appears in the pitch deck.

One caveat, and it is the important one. Exit length predicts nothing about selling. It is a ceiling on speed, not a forecast of direction, and a fund with a long exit may hold happily for a decade and never touch the position. What the figure tells you is what happens if they change their mind, which is a different question from whether they will. Read it as a constraint on the shape of any future exit and it becomes one of the most useful things you can compute from public data. Read it as a sell signal and you will be wrong in a way that costs you money.
